lesson.title: React useEffect() Hook Introduction
lesson.goal: learn the React useEffect hook: run side effects on mount and on state changes, and clean them up

steps.title: Set up React counter component
steps.instructions: In an empty folder, create a React Vite app with `npm create vite@latest my-react-app -- --template react`, install dependencies, and start it with `npm run dev`. In `src/MyComponent.jsx` (rendered from `src/App.jsx`), import `useState` and `useEffect` and build a counter with an Add button.

targets.caption: Create count state and an Add button

explanations.topic: What useEffect does and its three trigger modes

hints: Make sure you run npm install inside my-react-app before starting the dev server.
Import both useState and useEffect from "react" at the top of src/MyComponent.jsx.
Use the updater function setCount(c => c + 1) inside addCount and pass addCount to the button's onClick prop.
common_mistakes: Calling addCount() immediately in onClick={addCount()} instead of passing the function reference.
steps.code:
import React, {useState, useEffect} from "react"; function MyComponent() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); function addCount(){ setCount(c => c + 1); } return (<>

Count: {count}

); } export default MyComponent;

steps.title: Update document title on re-render
steps.instructions: Add a `useEffect` call near the top of `MyComponent` with an arrow function and no second argument. Inside it, set `document.title` to `` `Count: ${count}` `` so the browser tab title updates on every re-render.

explanations.topic: useEffect syntax without a dependency array
Why an empty dependency array runs only on mount

hints: Place useEffect near the top of your component function.
Pass only a single callback argument (() => { ... }) to run after every render.
Use backticks for the template string: document.title = `Count: ${count}`;
common_mistakes: Using regular quotes instead of backticks around `Count: ${count}`.
Placing useEffect inside a nested function or conditional instead of the top level of the component.

steps.title: Run effect only on mount
steps.instructions: In src/MyComponent.jsx, pass an empty array `[]` as the second argument to `useEffect` so the side effect runs only once on mount. Click Add in the browser to confirm the tab title no longer changes on re-renders.

targets.caption: Add an empty dependency array as the second argument

hints: Add a comma after the callback function inside useEffect(...).
Pass [] as the second argument: useEffect(() => { ... }, []);
common_mistakes: Putting [] inside the callback function body instead of as the second argument to useEffect.

steps.title: Trigger effect when count changes
steps.instructions: In src/MyComponent.jsx, put `count` in the `useEffect` dependency array `[count]` so the title updates on mount and whenever count changes. Add a `subtractCount` function and a Subtract button to verify both trigger the effect.

targets.caption: Include count in the dependency array

explanations.topic: Difference between [count] and omitting the dependency array

hints: Place count inside the square brackets of the dependency array.
Copy addCount, rename it to subtractCount, and change + 1 to - 1.
Add <button onClick={subtractCount}>Subtract</button> right after the Add button.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to pass the subtractCount handler to the new button's onClick prop.
steps.code: useEffect(() => { document.title = `Count: ${count}`; }, [count]); function subtractCount(){ setCount(c => c - 1); } <button onClick={subtractCount}>Subtract</button>

steps.title: Watch multiple state dependencies
steps.instructions: In src/MyComponent.jsx, create a `color` state initialized to "green" with a `changeColor` button toggling green/red, and style the count paragraph with `style={{color: color}}`. Include `${color}` in `document.title` and use `[count, color]` as dependencies.

targets.caption: Add color alongside count in the dependency array

explanations.topic: Why missing a dependency causes stale values in the title
Benefits of useEffect over bare top-level side effects

hints: Initialize color with const [color, setColor] = useState("green");.

Use a ternary inside setColor(c => c === "green" ? "red" : "green") and apply style={{color: color}} on the

tag.
Update both the template string in document.title and the dependency array to [count, color].
common_mistakes: Using single curly braces style={color: color} instead of double braces style={{color: color}} in JSX.
Using color in document.title without adding color to the dependency array.
steps.code:
const [color, setColor] = useState("green"); useEffect(() => { document.title = `Count: ${count} ${color}`; }, [count, color]); function changeColor(){ setColor(c => c === "green" ? "red" : "green"); }

Count: {count}

steps.title: Track window size on mount
steps.instructions:
In src/MyComponent.jsx, replace the counter with width and height states initialized from window.innerWidth and window.innerHeight, and show both in

tags. Define handleResize and register window.addEventListener("resize", handleResize) inside useEffect(..., []) so one listener is added on mount.

targets.caption: Attach the resize listener once inside useEffect with []

explanations.topic: Why adding event listeners outside useEffect leaks listeners
Why StrictMode runs useEffect twice in development

hints: Initialize width and height using window.innerWidth and window.innerHeight.
Write handleResize to call setWidth(window.innerWidth) and setHeight(window.innerHeight).
Wrap window.addEventListener("resize", handleResize) inside useEffect(() => { ... }, []).
common_mistakes: Calling handleResize() with parentheses in addEventListener instead of passing the function reference.
Omitting the empty [] dependency array, causing a new resize listener to be added on every resize.
steps.code:
const [width, setWidth] = useState(window.innerWidth); const [height, setHeight] = useState(window.innerHeight); useEffect(() => { window.addEventListener("resize", handleResize); console.log("EVENT LISTENER ADDED"); }, []); function handleResize(){ setWidth(window.innerWidth); setHeight(window.innerHeight); } return (<>

Window Width: {width}px

Window Height: {height}px

);

steps.title: Clean up resize event listener
steps.instructions: In src/MyComponent.jsx, return a cleanup arrow function from the resize `useEffect` callback. Inside it, call `window.removeEventListener("resize", handleResize)` and log a message such as "EVENT LISTENER REMOVED".

targets.caption: Return a cleanup function that removes the resize listener

explanations.topic: When the useEffect cleanup function runs
Observing StrictMode setup and cleanup in the console
Using multiple useEffect hooks in one component

hints: At the bottom of the useEffect callback, add a return statement.
Return an arrow function () => { ... } that calls window.removeEventListener.
Pass the same "resize" event name and handleResize callback to removeEventListener.
common_mistakes: Executing removeEventListener directly inside useEffect instead of returning a function that calls it.
Passing a different callback reference to removeEventListener than the one passed to addEventListener.
steps.code: return () => { window.removeEventListener("resize", handleResize); console.log("EVENT LISTENER REMOVED"); }

steps.title: Add second useEffect for title
steps.instructions: Add a second useEffect in src/MyComponent.jsx that depends on [width, height] and sets document.title to `Size: ${width} x ${height}`. Resize the browser window to see the tab title update.

targets.caption: Add a second useEffect watching width and height

hints: You can call useEffect more than once in the same React component.
Add a new useEffect(() => { ... }, [width, height]); below the resize listener effect.
Set document.title = `Size: ${width} x ${height}`; inside the new effect.
common_mistakes: Nesting the second useEffect inside the first useEffect instead of placing it at the top level of the component.
Forgetting to include both width and height in the dependency array.
